summary: The developer machine has the essential runtime (Node 24), the DocumentDB data-plane MCP server, Azure CLI signed-in, and a rich set of DocumentDB agent skills — enough to start implementing and verifying the Node.js + LlamaIndex sample. Gaps: embedding/LLM provider credentials and LlamaIndex bindings are not installed/verified; some command-line tools (mongosh, bicep, terraform, azd) are missing but only some are critical for convenient verification; several common model- and index-related facts in the cold answers were outdated or confused with older Cosmos or other vendors.
summary_points: All required DocumentDB agent skills and the documentdb MCP server are installed and reachable, so collection/index creation and run-time verification against the live cluster can proceed.
Runtime and Node toolchain are available (node, npx, npm) so the sample code, seed script and npm installs can be run locally.
Missing: an embedding/LLM provider integration and credentials (e.g., OpenAI key) and LlamaIndex Node bindings — these are required to build the embedding→DiskANN pipeline end-to-end.

Several cold answers were incorrect or outdated (resource type, CLI group, connection-string form, billing model, AAD data-plane auth, local emulator port) — builder must follow current DocumentDB docs (mongoClusters, az documentdb, vector-index createIndexes, Entra/OIDC examples).

Useful CLIs (mongosh) and IaC tools (bicep, terraform, azd) are absent; mongosh is worth adding for manual verification, IaC tools are helpful but optional because the sample uses an existing cluster.

tools.name: node / npm / npx
tools.needed_for: Run the Node.js sample, install npm dependencies (mongodb, llamaindex bindings, embedding client), and run seed and build scripts.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run or install the Node.js sample or seed scripts.

tools.name: documentdb MCP server (documentdb)
tools.needed_for: Data-plane verification: list databases, create collections/indexes, run createIndexes/create vector index commands, sample documents, explain query plans, and verify what the sample created on the live cluster.
tools.detail: documentdb MCP server with 18 data-plane tools (documentdb_list_databases, documentdb_create_index, documentdb_aggregate, etc.)
tools.impact_if_missing: Builder could not programmatically inspect collections/indexes or verify the cluster state; they'd be forced to rely on the portal or manual shell.
tools.workaround: Use the Azure portal or az CLI to inspect resources; but programmatic verification and run-time explains would be lost.

tools.name: Azure CLI (az)
tools.needed_for: Optional management / verification tasks (view cluster connection strings, enable features, update cluster auth modes), and useful for scripts to retrieve connection strings or to inspect resource metadata.
tools.detail: az CLI present (version 2.89.1) and signed-in (subscription available).
tools.impact_if_missing: Less convenient management and verification of the cluster; some scripted post-deploy checks would fail.
tools.workaround: Use the Azure portal; the documentdb MCP server covers many data-plane checks.

tools.name: Docker
tools.needed_for: Optional: run the local DocumentDB Gateway container for offline development if desired (gateway image exposes Mongo protocol on port 10260).
tools.detail: Docker installed (version 29.5.3). No local gateway running by default.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run a local DocumentDB gateway container for local-only tests; must test against the live cluster.
tools.workaround: Run and verify against the live cluster (the run environment explicitly expects that).

tools.name: mongosh
tools.needed_for: Convenient manual inspection and ad-hoc queries against the DocumentDB cluster (verify indexes, sample docs, change streams, run $search pipelines manually).
tools.impact_if_missing: Manual ad-hoc debugging will be harder (use Node scripts instead).
tools.workaround: Use small Node.js scripts with the mongodb driver or use the documentdb MCP tools to run queries; install mongosh if interactive shell is needed.

references.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Node.js

tools.name: OpenAI / embedding & LLM provider credentials
tools.needed_for: Generating product embeddings and producing LLM reasoning (LlamaIndex requires an embedding model and an LLM provider or local model).
tools.detail: No embedding/LLM provider credentials or provider bindings installed on the machine inventory; not part of the inventory.
tools.impact_if_missing: The embedding→DiskANN part and agent reasoning cannot be executed end-to-end; the sample would have to use mocked embeddings or skip the LLM reasoning.
tools.workaround: Use synthetic or deterministic embeddings in the seed script and stub the reasoning output in the UI; or require the builder to set OPENAI_API_KEY (or other provider env vars) and install the provider SDK.

tools.name: documentdb-driver (skill)
tools.needed_for: Guidance to instantiate the MongoClient properly (singleton pattern), driver connection tuning, and best practices for Node.js drivers when connecting to DocumentDB.
tools.impact_if_missing: Risk of incorrect connection usage (pool exhaustion, repeated clients).

tools.name: documentdb-vector-search (skill)
tools.needed_for: Index creation patterns (DiskANN/HNSW/IVF), recommended parameter values (dimensions, lBuild/lSearch/maxDegree), and guidance on query-time $search usage for vector queries.
tools.impact_if_missing: Risk of creating suboptimal vector indexes or querying them incorrectly.

tools.name: documentdb-local-deployment (skill)
tools.needed_for: Guidance for running a local DocumentDB gateway container (image, port 10260, TLS config) if the builder wants local dev parity.
tools.detail: Installed skill describing gateway image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) and port 10260.
tools.impact_if_missing: Less guidance for local container-based testing.
tools.workaround: Use the live cluster as the run-environment instructs.

tools.name: Azure MCP server (azure)
tools.needed_for: Control-plane operations and best-practice lookups; helpful for management-plane checks and templates.
tools.workaround: Use az CLI or the Azure portal.

tools.name: Microsoft Learn MCP (learn)
tools.needed_for: Authoritative Microsoft documentation search & fetch (used below to ground cold-answer corrections).
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to ground claims in official docs programmatically.
tools.workaround: Use the Azure portal or manual web lookups.

accelerators_missed: DocumentDB Agent Kit (accelerator that packages data-modeling, indexing, and sample templates) — install: npx skills add Azure/documentdb-agent-kit

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure Cosmos DB (the service historically called DocumentDB) uses the resource provider namespace Microsoft.DocumentDB and the main account resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts.
confusions.grounded_answer: The current, supported resource type for managed Azure DocumentDB clusters is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (resource provider Microsoft.DocumentDB). Use the mongoClusters resource (not databaseAccounts) for the vCore-based cluster API.
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn (templates): Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoclusters
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historical and naming overlap: older Cosmos DB examples and earlier ARM templates used Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts for Cosmos DB account resources. The new vCore-managed Mongo clusters use a different nested resource type (mongoClusters) under the same provider namespace.
confusions.build_risk: An IaC/CLI script that attempted to create Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts expecting the new vCore cluster API would create or modify a different account type (or fail). Deploy/automation would target the wrong resource shape.
improvements: Add a prominent note to the 'databaseAccounts' template reference and the older quickstarts: 'For managed Mongo clusters use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (see mongoclusters template), not databaseAccounts.'
On the mongoClusters reference page add an explicit 'Previously referenced as' note linking to any legacy instructions that still mention databaseAccounts so readers upgrade their scripts.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group (core CLI). Example create command: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRG --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus2 --default-consistency-level Session
confusions.grounded_answer: The correct CLI group for the vCore-managed DocumentDB clusters is az documentdb mongocluster (e.g., az documentdb mongocluster create). There is a dedicated az documentdb command group with mongocluster subcommands.
confusions.grounding_source: Azure CLI docs: az documentdb mongocluster

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB documentation and many examples used az cosmosdb for Cosmos DB 'account' resources. The new managed Mongo cluster API exposes its own CLI subgroup (az documentdb mongocluster). Shared provider names and the historical 'DocumentDB' branding cause the mix-up.

confusion_sources.title: Az cosmosdb CLI (older Cosmos DB commands)

confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb create will not create the vCore mongoClusters resource; scripts will either fail or create a different Cosmos DB account type.
improvements: Update any 'az cosmosdb' quickstarts that mention Mongo to link to 'az documentdb mongocluster' and provide a migration note.
Add a one-line migration helper in the Azure CLI docs that maps old az cosmosdb usage to az documentdb mongocluster for vCore clusters.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (top-level); MongoDB database and collection nested resource types are Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases and Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases/collections. Terraform (azurerm provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account (set kind = "MongoDB" and appropriate capabilities), plus azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_database and azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_collection for DBs and collections.
confusions.grounded_answer: The current resource type to deploy vCore-managed clusters is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters in ARM/Bicep. For Terraform, use the azapi or the azurerm provider resource that maps to Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (examples and AVMs reference 'mongoClusters' or azurerm_mongo_cluster / azapi). The nested database/collection resources are handled under the mongoClusters resource model now.
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn templates: Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historical ARM/Bicep abstractions for Cosmos DB used databaseAccounts and nested mongodbDatabases; the newer vCore-managed DocumentDB cluster API introduces mongoClusters as the top-level resource, which looks similar but is a different resource format.
confusions.build_risk: Using the older resource type in a Bicep/ARM template will not create the vCore mongoClusters resource expected by this sample; deployment templates and parameter shapes will be incorrect.
improvements: Add a 'When to use mongoClusters vs databaseAccounts' note to the databaseAccounts template page and to the 'Deploy with Bicep' quickstarts.

Add a Terraform/azapi snippet on the mongoClusters template page showing the exact provider mapping developers should use (azurerm_mongo_cluster or azapi with resourceType Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters).

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical MongoDB API connection string for a Cosmos account: either SRV form or standard. Example (standard TLS port): mongodb://<username>:<password>@myaccount.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retrywrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000&appName=@myaccount@. SRV form: mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@myaccount.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retrywrites=false. Host suffix: .mongo.cosmos.azure.com; port (non-SRV) 10255; required options include ssl=true (TLS), replicaSet=globaldb and typically retryWrites=false for Cosmos Mongo compatibility.
confusions.grounded_answer: For the vCore-managed Azure DocumentDB mongoClusters the SRV/URI form differs: examples and the CLI output show SRV endpoints like mongodb+srv://<user>:<password>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256&retrywrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000 (authMechanism and scheme differ). The 'global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com' host form and authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256 (or OIDC for Entra-auth) are the documented forms for mongoClusters. Do not assume the older .mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255 form.
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb-azure-deployment (skill) — connection string form and Azure CLI docs
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older Cosmos DB Mongo API used the host suffix .mongo.cosmos.azure.com and port 10255. The new vCore-managed DocumentDB clusters use a different host naming pattern (global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com) and different recommended options; the similar names cause mistaken copy/paste.

confusion_sources.title: Older Cosmos DB Mongo connection examples (databaseAccounts)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong connection string host/port or missing authMechanism will cause connection failures (TLS/auth errors) or mis-configured driver options. The sample's run-time config file and error messages must reflect the correct URI format.
improvements: On any quickstart that shows a connection string, add a bullet: 'For vCore-managed clusters (mongoClusters) use the mongoClusters SRV host form (global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com) and authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256 or OIDC; do not copy the old .mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255 example.'
Add an example in the Quickstart Node.js page showing how to populate DOCUMENTDB_URI from az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings output.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos (DocumentDB/Mongo API) is billed primarily with throughput (Request Units per second) for provisioned throughput accounts (including autoscale/auto-provisioning). There is also a serverless option for supported accounts and autoscale RU options. Recent offerings add vCore-based options for certain SKUs, but the canonical model for Mongo API samples is RU/s provisioned or serverless consumption.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore-managed Mongo clusters) is billed for compute (cluster tier measured in vCores for each shard) and provisioned storage; there is no RU/s model for this offering. The service uses cluster tiers (M10/M20/M30...) and storage per shard.
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn: Azure DocumentDB pricing (pricing-explained)
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Existing mental models for Cosmos DB Core (SQL) API use RU/s billing. People often assume Cosmos-like RU billing applies to all Cosmos-family offerings; the vCore-based DocumentDB product intentionally uses compute tiers and storage billing, not RUs.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB RU model docs

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes RUs, sample sizing and cost guidance will be wrong; scripts that attempt to set throughput via RU calls on the wrong resource type will fail.
improvements: On pages that mention Cosmos DB billing, add a short note: 'Note: vCore-managed Azure DocumentDB (mongoClusters) uses compute tiers (vCores) + storage; it does not use RU/s.'
Add a short example of converting from RU-oriented examples to vCore cluster-tier choices in the migration or quickstart docs.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Data-plane access for the MongoDB API is via MongoDB credentials (SCRAM username/password stored in the Cosmos account). Management operations use Azure AD (Microsoft Entra) via ARM roles. As of my knowledge cutoff, Entra ID based data-plane authentication (AAD token directly in the MongoDB driver) is not generally supported for the MongoDB API — drivers authenticate with the Mongo/SCRAM credentials; Azure AD is used for management/ARM operations. (Use standard MongoDB auth.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports both native (SCRAM) authentication and Microsoft Entra ID data-plane authentication (OIDC) for the Mongo protocol. You can enable Microsoft Entra ID (authMode MicrosoftEntraID) on a cluster and clients present an Entra-issued OIDC access token to the MongoDB driver (authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC). The docs describe enabling auth-allowed-modes and the SRV connection string pattern for OIDC connections.
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

grounding_links.title: How to connect: role-based access control (Microsoft Entra ID, OIDC)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos Mongo API accounts didn't offer Entra ID data-plane sign-in; the addition of OIDC/MicrosoftEntraID for the vCore clusters is a newer capability and is easy to miss.

confusion_sources.title: Older pages describing only SCRAM with Cosmos Mongo

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes only SCRAM, they may not implement OIDC flows when required by policy (managed identity scenarios), or may attempt to store long-lived passwords instead of using tokens for managed-identity based auth.
improvements: Add an explicit, top-level example in the 'connect' quickstarts showing the OIDC connection string and a short how-to: enable MicrosoftEntraID on the cluster, register the client identity, then connect with authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC.
Add an 'authModes' example in the az documentdb mongocluster create/update CLI docs listing NativeAuth and MicrosoftEntraID and showing the --auth-allowed-modes flag.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: For the data plane use the official MongoDB drivers (Node.js mongodb, pymongo, Java MongoDB driver, etc.) since Cosmos DB exposes the MongoDB wire protocol. There is no separate proprietary data-plane SDK for Mongo API; use azure-cosmos SDK only for Cosmos SQL API/other management scenarios and the az SDK for management operations.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use the official MongoDB drivers (e.g., npm package 'mongodb') for data-plane access to Azure DocumentDB. The quickstarts and driver examples use the mongodb Node.js driver. There is no separate DocumentDB-specific data-plane SDK for the Mongo API.
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn quickstarts and 'Use the MongoDB driver' guidance

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Node.js

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: If the cluster has vector capabilities enabled, index types exposed in samples include HNSW, IVF and DiskANN. The Mongo-style command to create a vector index is a createIndex call on the collection with a vector index spec; e.g. db.products.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { method: 'HNSW', dimensions: 1536, metric: 'cosine' }). (Note: exact option names vary by provider/version; treat this as the concrete form to try against the cluster.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports vector-ivf, vector-hnsw and vector-diskann index kinds. The documented way to create them is via the createIndexes runCommand payload (createIndexes with a cosmosSearchOptions block specifying kind, dimensions, similarity, and algorithm-specific params like numLists, m, efConstruction, maxDegree, lBuild). Example templates and the $search aggregation (cosmosSearch operator) are documented in the vector-search docs.
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (vector-search docs)

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB — vector index examples

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The MongoDB community createIndex signature is familiar and similar; DocumentDB exposes vector index creation via a createIndexes runCommand with DocumentDB-specific cosmosSearchOptions shape. The field names/structure differ from a naive createIndex call.
confusions.build_risk: A builder who uses the community createIndex call with method/metric fields will get an unsupported command or no-op; the index won't be created correctly and vector search will fail.
improvements: Show a small, copy-paste createIndexes runCommand JSON example on the Quickstart Node.js vector-search page for each index kind (IVF/HNSW/DiskANN) with default tuning parameters for the sample dataset size.
Add a short 'common mistakes' note: 'Do not use mongodb createIndex with method: HNSW — use createIndexes runCommand with cosmosSearchOptions.'

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Full-text and hybrid (text + vector) search for Cosmos DB data is typically accomplished by integrating with Azure Cognitive Search (Azure Search) or by using the service's built-in search features if the account offers integrated vector+text search. In practice you index documents into Azure Cognitive Search for rich textual ranking and combine that with vector search results for hybrid queries.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB includes integrated text search and vector search capabilities and supports hybrid queries (vector + text/geospatial filters) directly via the $search aggregation stage and the cosmosSearch operator; you do not have to use Azure Cognitive Search. Azure Cognitive Search is an optional external integration but is not required for the documented built-in hybrid capabilities.
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn: Integrated vector store and $search (cosmosSearch) docs

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB — hybrid and filtered vector search

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Many Azure examples combine Cosmos data with Azure Cognitive Search for richer text ranking historically; that pattern is still valid but DocumentDB now provides builtin text + vector capabilities, which is a different (and simpler) integration path. The similarity of 'search' terminology causes confusion.
confusions.build_risk: If a builder assumes Azure Cognitive Search is mandatory they may add an unnecessary external service and ETL pipeline, increasing complexity and cost.
improvements: On the vector-search quickstarts, add a short 'When to use Azure Cognitive Search' section clarifying that DocumentDB supports integrated text+vector hybrid queries and Azure Cognitive Search is optional for specialized ranking features.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos Mongo API exposes a MongoDB wire protocol version mapped to specific server versions; historically supported versions have included 3.6, 4.0, 4.2, 4.4 and later added 5.x/6.x in previews. Newer accounts may support 6.0/7.0 wire protocol in preview. Not all MongoDB server features are supported: server-side JavaScript, some aggregation stages or newer commands, multi-document transactions across partitions (transactions are limited to items in a single logical partition), and some admin commands may be unsupported or behave differently. Always check the account's configured MongoDB API version for exact feature availability.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore-managed) supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 and advertises broad MQL compatibility (99.03% of operators). Some administrative commands and some features differ from stock MongoDB; the docs provide a feature-compatibility matrix and a compatibility assessment tool.
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn: MongoDB compatibility and MQL compatibility pages

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold-answer mixed historical account versions and lacked the updated support matrix — versions supported evolved quickly and the vCore product supports modern wire protocol versions.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes an older server version or wrong unsupported features, queries or client-driver options may fail; test against target cluster wire version.
improvements: Add a short compatibility header on quickstarts: 'This tutorial targets mongo wire protocol X (e.g., 8.0); to use a different wire version, change serverVersion on cluster creation and review the compatibility table.'
Link the compatibility assessment tool (migration extension) more prominently in migration / quickstart docs.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is an Azure Cosmos DB Emulator (Windows and a Linux container image) but historically it primarily supports the SQL/Core API; MongoDB API compatibility in the emulator has been limited. For realistic MongoDB-protocol testing use a real Cosmos account or run a local MongoDB server (docker image mongo:latest) on port 27017 for driver-level development — but note behavior differs from Cosmos. If you must use an emulator, use the official Azure Cosmos DB Emulator (example container image mcr.microsoft.com/cosmosdb/linux/azure-cosmos-emulator) and confirm Mongo API support for your emulator version.
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB development the recommended local option is the DocumentDB Gateway Docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) which exposes the MongoDB wire protocol on port 10260 (TLS + SCRAM-SHA-256). The documentdb-local-deployment skill documents using that gateway image and port 10260 for local dev. The Cosmos DB emulator is not the recommended path for vCore DocumentDB local testing.
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb-local-deployment (skill)
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Confusion between the Azure Cosmos DB emulator (which historically focused on Core/SQL API) and the DocumentDB Gateway container; both are 'emulator-like' but different projects with different ports and capabilities.
confusions.build_risk: If the developer tries to use the Cosmos emulator or a stock Mongo image on port 27017 they will see behavioral differences and possibly miss DocumentDB-specific features (vector search on port 10260, TLS quirks).
improvements: Add a short 'Local development' note to the Quickstart top matter that explicitly says: 'To run DocumentDB locally use the DocumentDB Gateway image (port 10260) — see documentdb-local-deployment skill' so readers don't try the Cosmos emulator by mistake.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change stream support depends on the MongoDB API compatibility level of the Cosmos account. In many supported versions Cosmos offers change stream-like functionality but historically change streams were not fully supported or were limited; some accounts/versions now support change streams. No special portal toggle is usually required beyond having the appropriate MongoDB server compatibility version enabled on the account. (Check the account's MongoDB feature/version for exact support.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports change streams; for multishard clusters there is a feature toggle to enable 'Change streams for multishard clusters' (preview) and the docs describe enabling it via the cluster Features panel. Single-shard change streams are supported by default; multi-shard cross-shard change streams require enabling the feature and certain preconditions.
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historical limitations and preview semantics for multi-shard change streams created uncertainty; the new service documents explicit enabling steps for multishard scenarios.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes change streams are always available across shards, an online migration or a multi-shard reactive pipeline may miss the required feature toggle and produce incomplete change event coverage.
improvements: On the change-streams page add a short checklist: 'For single-shard: supported by default. For multi-shard: disable Rebalancer, enable 'Change streams for multishard clusters' in Features, then register any managed identities.'

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the service-specific 'documentdb' MCP server profile (the skill_md refers to a documentdb MCP profile named default) for data-plane inspection tools. The general Azure MCP server covers management plane (ARM) operations, but for collection-level data-plane inspection the documentdb MCP server/profile is the one to use.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the 'documentdb' MCP server provides data-plane tools (list DBs, find, aggregate, createIndex, explain, etc.). The 'azure' MCP server covers control-plane/management tasks. Use the documentdb MCP server (connection_profile 'default') for data-plane queries and index management.
confusions.grounding_source: machine inventory (documentdb MCP server listed) and the documentdb MCP tool descriptions

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Microsoft originally marketed the service as Azure DocumentDB. It was rebranded/expanded into Azure Cosmos DB (a multi-model globally distributed database). The Cosmos DB service exposes multiple APIs including SQL (Core), MongoDB-compatible API, Cassandra, Gremlin and Table. The name DocumentDB in other contexts (open-source projects or AWS DocumentDB) is unrelated; Azure DocumentDB was the precursor name for Cosmos DB's document model.
confusions.grounded_answer: This is a common source of historical confusion. The current managed product 'Azure DocumentDB' (the vCore-managed MongoDB-compatible service) was previously offered as 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)'. Separately, 'Azure Cosmos DB' historically came from the DocumentDB-era branding; the new vCore offering reintroduced the name 'Azure DocumentDB' for a first-party vCore product built on the open-source DocumentDB engine. The open-source 'DocumentDB' engine (github.com/documentdb) is the engine that this managed service is built on; Amazon DocumentDB is an unrelated AWS product with the same name.
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn migration and compare docs

grounding_links.title: Compare Azure DocumentDB with Amazon DocumentDB / migration note
Moving from another MongoDB-compatible service to Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The brand names have changed over time; 'DocumentDB' was a historical Azure product name and was reused in different contexts (open-source engine versus earlier Cosmos branding versus the new vCore offering), causing ambiguity.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong historical name in automation or docs can lead to referencing the wrong templates, CLI commands or API shapes.
improvements: Add a short timeline cross-reference in the product docs: 'DocumentDB (original) → Cosmos DB → Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore) → Azure DocumentDB (vCore). If you see 'databaseAccounts' or 'CosmosDB for MongoDB (vCore)' in older docs, use mongoClusters in current APIs.'

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: The underlying engine is Cosmos DB's proprietary distributed storage/compute engine that translates or implements the MongoDB wire protocol. In practice you use standard MongoDB drivers and application code is largely unchanged, but server behavior/limits differ (partitioning, RU model, some unsupported commands, transactional limits and subtle differences in query/aggregation semantics).
confusions.grounded_answer: The vCore-managed Azure DocumentDB service is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (https://github.com/documentdb/documentdb) and includes the MongoDB wire protocol compatibility layer. For application code: use standard MongoDB drivers, but expect DocumentDB-specific differences (limits, admin commands, integrated vector/text search). The underlying engine being open-source means the same engine can run locally and on-prem, and some operational behaviors differ from a stock MongoDB server.
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn compare/migration docs and documentdb-azure-deployment skill

grounding_links.title: Compare Azure DocumentDB with Amazon DocumentDB / engine notes

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: People often assume 'Cosmos DB' implies the Cosmos proprietary engine; the vCore product revived the DocumentDB engine (open-source) under the Azure DocumentDB name which differs from Cosmos DB Core in operational model and billing.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming the Cosmos proprietary engine semantics (RUs, certain admin behaviors) could lead to incorrect capacity/provisioning code and tests.
improvements: Add a clear 'engine' statement at the top of the Azure DocumentDB overview page: 'This service uses the open-source DocumentDB engine; it is not the same runtime as Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts).' Provide a small table of practical differences (billing, auth, indexing).

confusions.question: Where should the sample read the Azure DocumentDB connection string from at runtime?
confusions.cold_answer: Read the connection string from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime. If DOCUMENTDB_URI is missing or empty the app should exit with a clear error message telling the user to set DOCUMENTDB_URI (or populate a config file) instead of continuing.
confusions.grounded_answer: This sample's run environment specifies using the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI to hold the cluster connection string at runtime. If it is missing the application should display a clear error and refuse to proceed (or prompt). Use a .env.example with a placeholder and never commit the real secret.
confusions.grounding_source: Sample run-environment instructions (provided to the build environment)

confusions.question: What database name and collections will this sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the database named sample_retail_02 for all sample data. Create collections named transactions (holds purchase transactions) and products (product metadata).
confusions.grounded_answer: The run-environment for this sample specifies the database sample_retail_02. Standard sample layout can use collections transactions (or purchases) and products; pick simple names and keep everything inside sample_retail_02 to avoid touching other DBs.
confusions.grounding_source: Sample run-environment instructions (provided to the build environment)

confusions.question: Which Node.js client and connection invocation will the sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the official Node.js MongoDB driver (npm package mongodb). Connect with MongoClient: const client = new MongoClient(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { tls: true, useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true }); await client.connect(); Then use client.db('sample_retail_02').collection('transactions') etc.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the official mongodb npm package and follow the documentdb-driver skill guidance: instantiate a singleton MongoClient with TLS enabled and appropriate driver options (e.g., authMechanism set as needed), await client.connect(), and reuse the client across modules.
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn Quickstart + documentdb-driver skill

confusions.question: What vector index definition will the sample create for nearest-neighbour search?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a vector index on the embedding field with a method and dimensions; for example: db.transactions.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { method: 'HNSW', dimensions: 1536, metric: 'cosine' }). (If the cluster supports DiskANN or IVF, swap method accordingly. Use this form as the index create command to run against the cluster.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Create a DocumentDB vector index using the createIndexes runCommand JSON and cosmosSearchOptions.kind set to 'vector-hnsw' / 'vector-ivf' / 'vector-diskann' and dimensions matching the chosen embedding model (e.g., 1536). Use the documented parameter names (numLists, m, efConstruction, maxDegree, lBuild/lSearch etc.) rather than a MongoDB createIndex options object.
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn: vector search examples (createIndexes + cosmosSearchOptions)

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB — create index templates

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The builder's MongoDB intuition uses createIndex option shapes; DocumentDB requires the createIndexes runCommand with cosmosSearchOptions shape.
confusions.build_risk: Creating the index with the wrong API will fail or create a non-functional index; vector queries will not return expected nearest neighbours.
improvements: Provide a copy-paste createIndexes runCommand snippet for the sample's collection (HNSW and DiskANN variants) and a line that says 'use dimensions = <embedding-dimension>' to avoid model-index mismatches.

confusions.question: How should the ingestion script load 20,000 purchase transactions efficiently?
confusions.cold_answer: Use bulk inserts in batches (e.g., batches of 500–1000 documents). In Node.js use collection.insertMany(batch, { ordered: false }) or bulkWrite with unordered operations. Include fields: { transactionId, userId, items: [ productId, qty ], timestamp, embedding: [float...] } and commit batches sequentially to avoid request size/timeouts.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: seed in batches using insertMany or bulkWrite with unordered operations, keep batch sizes reasonable (500–1000) to avoid request-size/timeouts, and populate transaction schema fields. If embeddings are computed client-side, create embeddings in parallel with throttling and add them to the documents before bulk insert.
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb-vector-search and documentdb-local-deployment guidance + Node quickstart best-practices

information_gaps.title: Embedding model & dimension
information_gaps.description: The prompt requires generating product embeddings but does not specify the embedding model (provider and model name) or dimensionality. This determines the vector index 'dimensions' parameter. I searched the Microsoft docs and installed skills but did not find any recommendation to pick a default model or env var name for embeddings. Looked at: Microsoft Learn vector-search docs, documentdb-vector-search skill, prompt run-environment notes.

information_gaps.title: LLM provider & LlamaIndex Node bindings
information_gaps.description: The prompt asks for a LlamaIndex agent in Node.js but does not name which LLM provider or Node bindings (package names/versions) should be used. The agent runtime and code examples depend on which LlamaIndex Node SDK and LLM model are selected. I searched the run environment and installed skills but those do not include LlamaIndex examples; looked at Microsoft docs and skills but found no LlamaIndex Node bindings guidance.

information_gaps.title: Agent memory persistence format
information_gaps.description: Prompt requires per-session personalized recommendations via agent memory. The builder needs to choose where to store session memory (in-process, browser sessionStorage, Redis, or a DocumentDB collection). No skill or doc in the inventory prescribes which approach to choose for this sample; I searched documentdb skills and quickstarts for session-store guidance and found none specific to agent-memory persistence.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource and the az documentdb mongocluster CLI for any cluster-level management; do not rely on Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts for vCore-managed clusters.

Create vector indexes with the createIndexes runCommand JSON and cosmosSearchOptions.kind set to 'vector-diskann' or 'vector-hnsw' (and set dimensions to match your embedding model). Do not attempt to create DocumentDB vector indexes with a community createIndex options object.
